source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items when the format is right. Calibration improves with model size and from zero-shot to few-shot.
numbers: Anthropic models up to 52B. Replacing an option with 'none of the above' reduced accuracy and calibration significantly (their Fig 7).
limits: Format-dependent: calibration does not carry to open-ended generation without extra steps.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a model's raw confidence is usable on free-form answers.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know (P(True))
finding: Ask the model to propose an answer, then score P(True) that it is correct. This works on open tasks and improves when the model sees many of its own samples before judging one.
numbers: Tasks: GSM8k, arithmetic, TriviaQA, Lambada, Codex. Accuracy rises when conditioning on P(True) > 0.5 (their figure).
limits: Needs logit access and a 52B-class model. P(True) is an internal probability, not a stated number.
agent_relevance: Self-evaluation is better when it sees several samples: supports sample-based checks over single self-report.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know (P(IK))
finding: A trained head predicts 'I know the answer' without seeing an answer. It does well in-distribution but is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: 52B P(IK) AUROC / Brier, trained on all tasks: Lambada 0.864/0.151; Python function synthesis 0.928/0.194; one task as low as 0.606/0.431.
limits: Training required. Out-of-distribution calibration is weak. P(IK) rises when relevant source text or hints are in context.
agent_relevance: Pre-answer 'can I solve this' routing needs training; a prompt alone is not shown to do it.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 fine-tuned to state a confidence (number or word) on CalibratedMath stays calibrated under distribution shift. First demonstration of verbalized confidence.
numbers: Fine-tuned verbalized number, Multi-answer: MSE 22.0 vs constant baseline 37.4 (their Table 1; lower is better). Multiply-divide: 10.4 vs constant 11.7.
quote: Both kinds of uncertainty are capable of generalizing calibration under distribution shift.
limits: Needed fine-tuning. Gain over a constant baseline on multiply-divide is small. Only GPT-3 and arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence is learned, not free. Zero-shot self-report cannot be assumed calibrated.

source: Lin et al. (2022) heuristic and logit controls
finding: Authors checked that verbalized calibration is not explained by copying logits or by simple heuristics such as the size of the integers in the question.
numbers: Their Section 3.4.
quote: This calibration performance is not explained by learning to output logits.
limits: GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence carried information beyond logits there, a point for hybrid signals.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, verbalized confidence is better calibrated than the model's token probabilities. Prompting for several answer choices first (considering the opposite) improves it further.
numbers: On ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude 2 across three datasets, verbalized confidence plus temperature scaling often cut ECE by over 50% versus token probabilities.
limits: ECE can be gamed: a constant 50% output has perfect ECE on binary tasks, so they also report AUC. Temperature scaling needs labelled data.
agent_relevance: Calibration is not discrimination. Check both before trusting a stated number.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Benchmark of black-box confidence methods on 5 LLMs and 8+ datasets. Verbalized confidence is overconfident, clustered at 80-100% in multiples of 5, as in human text.
numbers: GPT-4 vanilla verbalized AUROC averages only 62.7% (chance 50%). GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns
limits: Even the best method is far from ideal. White-box gap is narrow: AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for SCHEMA 4b: self-reported certainty is weak for stopping.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) sampling and consistency
finding: Agreement across 5 sampled answers beats verbalized confidence for failure prediction. On the arithmetic task AUROC went from 54.8% (near chance) to 92.7%. Gains rise with number of samples then plateau (tested M=1 to 13).
numbers: GPT-3.5, CoT prompt, M=5, consistency aggregation (their Table 3).
limits: Task-specific: the jump is quoted for arithmetic. Consistency cannot separate confidently wrong answers shared by all samples.
agent_relevance: Use sample agreement as the confidence signal. Five samples already give most of the gain.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) human-inspired prompts
finding: Prompts borrowed from human metacognition (step-wise confidence, top-K alternatives, CoT) give consistent but modest gains in calibration. No single strategy wins on all datasets and models. Gains shrink on GPT-4.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-4 at 93.6% accuracy reaches ECE 0.064 just by saying 100% every time, so low ECE can hide zero discrimination.
limits: Gains are partial and diminish with stronger models.
agent_relevance: Prompting for 'be more calibrated' is a weak lever. Do not rely on it.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
finding: The share of sampled chains that agree with the final vote is highly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K. Low agreement means low confidence.
numbers: Figure 5, GSM8K. With an imperfect prompt greedy accuracy fell 17.1 to 14.9 and self-consistency recovered the loss (their Table 8).
quote: self-consistency confers some ability for the model to "know when it doesn't know".
limits: Correlation shown in a figure, PaLM/GPT-3 era models. Shared systematic errors stay invisible.
agent_relevance: Founding result for using sample agreement as a stand-in for confidence.

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty
finding: Semantic entropy groups sampled answers by meaning (bidirectional entailment) and takes entropy over meanings. It predicts correctness better than token-level entropy because wording variation is not uncertainty.
numbers: AUROC semantic entropy vs count of distinct answers: CoQA 0.77 vs 0.66; TriviaQA 0.83 vs 0.79. Wrong answers had 1.77 vs 1.27 distinct meanings (CoQA) and 3.89 vs 1.89 (TriviaQA).
limits: Needs an extra entailment model and several samples. Gain over a simple distinct-count is modest (0.04 to 0.11 AUROC).
agent_relevance: A cheap form: cluster own samples by final answer and use the number and mass of clusters.

source: Farquhar et al. (2024) Detecting hallucinations in LLMs using semantic entropy (Nature)
finding: Pointer only: extends semantic entropy to longer free-form answers. Page was not readable (login redirect), so no numbers are recorded.
numbers: not opened
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Same idea as c11 in peer-reviewed form.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking the model to review its own answer lowers accuracy. With oracle labels it looks good, which is the flaw in earlier reports.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) to 41.8 (round 2). GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and flips correct to wrong more often than wrong to correct.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only. Oracle-label correction raised accuracy, so the failure is a missing reliable signal. Table columns parsed from a two-column PDF.
agent_relevance: A model's own judgment of its answer is a bad trigger to revise. Revision needs an external check.

source: Huang et al. (2024) debate versus self-consistency
finding: At matched numbers of responses, multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency.
numbers: GSM8K (their Table 7, as parsed): standard 76.7; self-consistency 82.5 at 3, 85.3 at 6, 88.2 at 9 responses; debate about 83 at similar budgets.
limits: One paper, GPT-3.5. Row alignment of the table is approximate.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 (no debate) and voting over mutual critique.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Relying on the Unreliable: Language Model Expressions of Uncertainty
finding: Deployed LMs rarely hedge even when wrong. When prompted for confidence they are overconfident: about 47% error among confident answers. Human users rely on the output whether or not it is hedged.
numbers: Average 47% error rate among confident responses. Alignment preference data: uncertainty expressions in 5.02% of rejected vs 4.47% of chosen texts.
limits: Human-user part is a crowd experiment.
agent_relevance: Alignment training pushes models away from honest hedging, so self-report is biased upward.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know
finding: A calibration gap exists between the model's internal confidence and the confidence people read from its explanations. Longer explanations raise user confidence without improving accuracy. Matching explanation tone to internal confidence narrows both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap.
numbers: Behavioral experiments with MMLU multiple-choice and short-answer questions. Metrics ECE and AUC. Exact gap sizes were not extracted.
quote: longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy
limits: Human participants, not agents.
agent_relevance: Long reasoning text makes confidence look higher to readers and perhaps to LLM judges: ties to G10.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) link to Fleming and Lau (2014)
finding: The LLM field scores confidence with AUC, which Steyvers et al. state parallels psychology measures of metacognitive discrimination (Fleming and Lau 2014). ECE tracks calibration or bias, a separate quantity.
numbers: Two axes: calibration (ECE) and discrimination (AUC).
limits: The mapping is by analogy. meta-d' (which corrects for task performance) was not used in the LLM papers opened.
agent_relevance: Report both axes for any confidence signal in the agent, and do not compare AUC across tasks of unequal difficulty.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone is not enough for calibrated uncertainty. Fine-tuning on about 1000 graded answers with LoRA beats prompt baselines in ECE and AUROC and generalizes across shifts.
numbers: LLaMA-2 7B/13B, Mistral 7B and chat variants, on a new open-ended MMLU. 1000 graded examples were sufficient.
limits: Needs weights and graded data. Open models only.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold-only agent, the ceiling of prompt-only calibration is low.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection
finding: A model fine-tuned to predict its own behavior beats a stronger model trained on the same data about it. This is a test of privileged self-access.
numbers: Llama-3-70B predicting itself beat GPT-4o predicting Llama-3-70B by +17% accuracy. Self-predictions were also better calibrated.
limits: Works on simple behaviours. Fails on tasks needing long outputs such as writing a story. Trained introspection did not generalize to self-awareness tasks.
agent_relevance: Self-knowledge exists but is narrow. Do not extend it to judging a long solution.

source: Anthropic (2025) Emergent introspective awareness in large language models
finding: When a concept is injected into activations, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 sometimes notice and name it. Peak effect about two thirds of the way through the layers.
numbers: About 20% of trials at the best layer and strength. 0 false positives over 100 trials in production models, though some helpful-only variants had false positives. Only the first 100k of 403k characters were read.
quote: The abilities we observe are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
limits: Artificial injection. Authors say transfer to normal use is unclear and extra detail may be confabulated.
agent_relevance: Real but rare introspection. Not a basis for trusting self-report.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weighting each sampled chain by the model's own confidence in a majority vote needs fewer samples than plain voting. Tested on 9 models and 4 datasets.
numbers: Over 40% fewer reasoning paths on average. With P(True), self-consistency needs 18.6 samples to match CISC at 10: a 46% cost reduction. Gemma2-9B on MATH: up to 73% in their Fig 1.
quote: Surprisingly, the most calibrated confidence method is actually the least useful for CISC.
limits: Confidence is used to rank answers to the same question, not to stop. Standard calibration metrics do not predict benefit, so they propose Within-Question Discrimination (WQD).
agent_relevance: Within-question ranking is the right test for a select signal, not average ECE.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling when the answers so far show a clear majority by a Bayesian stopping rule. This saves budget with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs: sample budget cut by up to 7.9 times with average accuracy drop below 0.1%.
limits: 7.9x is the best case. Early samples that agree on a wrong answer still stop the loop wrongly.
agent_relevance: Ready design for agreement-based stopping in an agent loop (G4, G12).

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses token-level log-prob confidence over sliding groups to filter weak reasoning traces and stop them early, then votes weighted by confidence.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025: 99.9% (DeepConf@512) vs 97.0% majority vote (cons@512) vs 91.8% pass@1. Up to 84.7% fewer tokens in online mode. Averaged over 64 repetitions per setting.
limits: Needs logprobs and a threshold set by an offline warmup. 512 traces per question is large. The 99.9% figure is the offline mode.
agent_relevance: Local step-level confidence from the token stream works where global self-report does not, if logprobs are available.

source: Synthesis across opened papers (Xiong 2024, Wang 2023, Taubenfeld 2025, Fu 2025)
finding: The picture is stable. Stated certainty is weak, while agreement among samples and token-level confidence carry the signal. The two can be combined in weighted votes.
numbers: Chance AUROC is 50%. Verbalized: 54.8% (arithmetic) and 62.7% (GPT-4 mean). Consistency: 92.7% on arithmetic.
limits: Numbers come from different models and tasks.
agent_relevance: Matches SCHEMA 4b: use sample consistency, not self-report.

source: Griot et al. (2025) Large language models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning (Nature Communications)
finding: Pointer only: a medical-reasoning test of metacognition in LLMs. Page not readable (login redirect), so no findings or numbers recorded.
numbers: not opened
limits: Not read. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Candidate test: trap items where the right answer is absent.
